design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis, written for the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine GRACE guideline programme, of direct evidence on topical capsaicin and dopamine antagonists (haloperidol, droperidol) for adults with cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) in emergency departments, against usual care or no active comparator. Seven studies, 492 patients: two randomized trials (59 patients), two retrospective cohort studies (244), two retrospective chart reviews (133) and one retrospective observational study (56); five on capsaicin (386) and two on dopamine antagonists (106). Narrative synthesis with study-level tables.
can_establish: What the few direct studies up to March 2022 report on capsaicin cream and on dopamine antagonists for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome treated in emergency departments, and how weak that evidence is.
cannot_establish: Pooled effect sizes (no meta-analysis), whether either treatment works better than standard antiemetics in a definitive trial, how CHS should be diagnosed, anything about treatment outside emergency departments, or about stopping cannabis, hot showers or other self-care measures (outside the review question).

sample.recruitment: Ovid MEDLINE to 24 March 2022, APA PsycInfo to March 2022, Cochrane CENTRAL (November 2021) and Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and Scopus; search designed by a medical librarian (Appendix S1, not read); reference lists of relevant reviews screened (p. 494).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed original articles in English; adults 18 or older presenting to an urgent care or emergency department for CHS; pharmacological treatment with a control group (usual care, no active comparator or head-to-head drugs). Excluded: no published results, no control or comparison group, reviews and guidelines, inaccessible full texts, non-ED settings (Table 1, p. 495).
sample.demographics: Study-level only (Tables 2 and 3): median or mean ages around 27 to 35; one cohort included patients from age 16; one trial's sample was about 90% African American.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; both randomized trials were judged at high risk of bias because of loss to follow-up (p. 498).
sample.selection_effects: English only; no trial registries searched for unpublished results (registered trials without results were excluded); few studies, mostly single-centre retrospective chart reviews in North America, some during the COVID-19 pandemic (p. 502).

exposure.measurement: Treatments as recorded in charts or given in trials; CHS defined differently across studies (for example recurrent vomiting with cannabis use, a coded diagnosis, or criteria such as hot-shower relief) (Tables 2 and 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 496-500): capsaicin cream 0.025% to 0.1% (one study also 0.15%), applied to the abdomen, amount often not measured; intravenous droperidol, median 2.19 mg (interquartile range 1.25-4.69); intravenous haloperidol printed as 0.05 mg or 0.1 mg (pooled), against intravenous ondansetron 8 mg; capsaicin against placebo cream in the other trial.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed; patients often received several other antiemetics, opioids or benzodiazepines, not standardized (Tables 2 and 3).

comparison.controls: Placebo cream (one trial), ondansetron (one trial), patients not given the study drug, the same patients' earlier visits, or pre-treatment pain scores.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity and duration of cannabis use and of symptoms often missing from charts (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: Nausea and pain visual analogue scales, need for rescue medicines, length of emergency department or hospital stay, admission, return visits, adverse events.
outcomes.validity_norms: Outcome definitions differed between studies; one cohort defined efficacy as needing at most one further drug.
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit judged from each study's own outcomes and significance tests.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative synthesis of six outcome types).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Two independent reviewers for title and abstract screening; risk-of-bias disagreements resolved by discussion; extraction procedure not described as duplicate.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Capsaicin trial (Dean et al., 2020, about 30 patients): nausea at 30 min not different from placebo cream (difference -2.0 cm, 95% CI printed as 0.2 to -4.2); complete resolution 29.4% against 0% (risk ratio printed 3.4, 1.6 to 7.1); lower mean nausea at 60 min; no difference in disposition or rescue antiemetics. Capsaicin cohorts: efficacy 55% against 21% (p<0.001) and time to discharge 3.72 against 6.11 h (Kum et al.); no change in pain scores before and after (Lee and Coralic); no difference in length of stay, 179 against 201 min (Wagner et al.); no difference in stay, medicines or return within 72 h and admissions 8 against 1 (Yusuf et al.). Haloperidol trial (Ruberto et al., 2021, 30 patients): greater improvement in pain and nausea at 2 h than ondansetron (mean difference 2.3 cm, p = 0.01), treatment success 54% against 29%, rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%, time to discharge 3.1 against 5.6 h (p = 0.03). Droperidol chart review (Lee et al., 2019, 76 patients): hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The review says it followed its protocol (p. 494), but no registration or published protocol is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: Risk-of-bias assessments only in an appendix (not read); no certainty-of-evidence rating, although the review was written for a guideline programme.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Capsaicin: one small placebo-controlled trial negative on its primary outcome with some secondary benefit, and four non-randomized studies split between modest benefit and no difference, one with more admissions after capsaicin. Dopamine antagonists: one small randomized trial against ondansetron and one chart review, both favouring the dopamine antagonist, with acute dystonia in three patients across the two. All evidence at moderate to high risk of bias.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion describe the evidence as limited, mixed for capsaicin and potentially beneficial (conclusion: positive support) for dopamine antagonists (pp. 493, 502), and call for rigorous trials; the Discussion adds that capsaicin's ease of use may justify a place in management (p. 501). The summary is broadly faithful; positive support for dopamine antagonists rests on two small studies, one non-randomized, and the haloperidol trial compared against ondansetron, an active usual-care drug.

timeline.event: Ruberto et al. (HaVOC), the randomized trial of haloperidol against ondansetron included in this review.
This review, for the SAEM GRACE guideline programme.

replication.where_it_stands: A small evidence base summarized carefully; the authors mention an ongoing randomized trial of capsaicin (NCT04283292) and an interim report comparing droperidol with haloperidol. Claims must not cite Ruberto et al. (2021) and this review as independent support.

funding.funder: Partly funded by the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine to answer a question set by its GRACE writing team; one author supported by the Peter Boris Chair in Addictions Research and a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair (p. 502).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 502); the funding statement also says one author is a principal in Beam Diagnostics, Inc. and a consultant to Clairvoyant Therapeutics, Inc.
funding.affiliations_note: McMaster University and St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton (Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research; Michael G. DeGroote Centre for Medicinal Cannabis Research).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered randomized trials in emergency departments comparing capsaicin, haloperidol or droperidol with standard antiemetics, using an agreed CHS definition, prespecified symptom outcomes at fixed times, return visits and adverse events, and follow-up of cannabis use afterwards.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, interventions, comparators and outcomes stated in PICO form.
A protocol is mentioned but not registered, cited or described.
Randomized and non-randomized studies were both admitted without a stated reason.
Several databases and a librarian-designed strategy, but English only without justification, no trial registries or grey literature, and studies without published results excluded.
Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts; discrepancies discussed with senior authors.

domains.note: The flow diagram gives counts by reason (for example 12 reviews or commentaries, one without a control group) but no list.

domains.note: Tables 2 and 3 give design, population, intervention details, control, outcomes and preliminary risk-of-bias notes for every study.

domains.note: MAGIC tool for cohort and chart-review studies and a Cochrane tool for trials, with summaries in the text and tables; full assessments only in appendices not read.

domains.note: Funding and author interests reported, although the no-conflicts statement sits beside two commercial roles of one author.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no registered protocol, a restricted search, no list of excluded studies), so AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. The review is nevertheless a clear, conservative description of a very small literature, and its tables let each study be traced. It can be cited for what the seven studies reported and for the weakness of the evidence; not for an effect size or as proof that either treatment works.

key_findings.finding: Included: 7 of 25 full texts (53 records): two randomized trials (59 patients), two retrospective cohort studies (244), two retrospective chart reviews (133) and one retrospective observational study (56), 492 patients in all; five studies of capsaicin (386 patients) and two of dopamine antagonists (106).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 493); Results, Study selection and characteristics (p. 495); Fig. 1

key_findings.finding: Capsaicin, randomized trial (Dean et al.): nausea 30 min after the cream did not differ from placebo cream (difference -2.0 cm, CI printed as 0.2 to -4.2); a higher proportion had complete resolution of nausea, 29.4% against 0% (risk ratio printed 3.4, 1.6 to 7.1); mean nausea was lower at 60 min; disposition and rescue antiemetics did not differ. The exclusion criteria were changed midway through recruitment.
key_findings.locator: Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (p. 498, right column); Table 3, Dean et al. row (p. 500)

key_findings.finding: Capsaicin, non-randomized studies: Kum et al. (201 patients) found more patients needing at most one further drug with capsaicin (55% against 21%, p<0.001) and a shorter time to discharge (3.72 against 6.11 h), with the review noting the capsaicin group had already received more drugs; Lee and Coralic (57, before-and-after) found no significant change in pain scores and no adverse drug events; Wagner et al. (43, compared with their own earlier visits) found no difference in length of stay (179 against 201 min, p = 0.33) but fewer additional medicines; Yusuf et al. (56, capsaicin available or not depending on the pharmacist on duty) found no difference in stay, medicines, 72-hour returns or admission rate, with 8 admissions after capsaicin against 1 without.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (pp. 496-499); Results, Studies on topical capsaicin (pp. 498-499)

key_findings.finding: Haloperidol trial (Ruberto et al., 30 patients, against ondansetron, the two haloperidol doses pooled): greater reduction in abdominal pain and nausea at 2 h (mean difference 2.3 cm, p = 0.01), treatment success 54% against 29%, rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%, benzodiazepines 8% against 41%, any medicine 31% against 76%, time to discharge 3.1 (SD 1.7) against 5.6 (SD 4.5) h (p = 0.03); two return visits for acute dystonia after haloperidol and none after ondansetron.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, Ruberto et al. row (p. 500); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501, left column)

key_findings.finding: Droperidol chart review (Lee et al., 76 patients): total hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014) and time to discharge after the last antiemetic 137 against 185 min (p = 0.002); two patients drowsy, one acute dystonia that responded to benztropine, no cardiac events.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Lee et al. row (pp. 496-497); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501)

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias: both randomized trials high, mainly because of loss to follow-up; retrospective studies low to high, most moderate to high.

The authors' conclusion: limited direct evidence, mixed support for capsaicin and positive but preliminary support for dopamine antagonists; capsaicin is not known to have serious side effects though application may be uncomfortable, while dystonia, arrhythmias and drowsiness are noted for dopamine antagonists.

reporting_issues.issue: For Kum et al., Table 2 gives an odds ratio of 0.2881 (p = 0.0070) for efficacy with symptoms of a month or longer against under a week, that is, lower odds, while the text says symptoms over a month had a significantly higher likelihood of relief (p. 499); the nausea odds ratio is 2.478 (p = 0.0285) in Table 2 and 2.626 (p = 0.036) in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Who benefits from capsaicin in that cohort cannot be cited from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 reports for Dean et al. a significantly higher rate of complete resolution of nausea (29.4% against 0%) and, among secondary outcomes, no significant difference in complete relief of nausea; a risk ratio of 3.4 with a finite interval is printed for a comparison with zero events in one arm; the control group is printed as n = 1 although the trial had about 29 patients, 17 on capsaicin.
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial's secondary results should be taken from the primary paper, not the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria require a control group and the flow diagram excludes one study for having none (Fig. 1), yet a before-and-after study without a control group (Lee and Coralic) is included; the text calls the five non-randomized studies uncontrolled although four had comparison groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in how designs are described.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name RoB 2 for trials but cite the 2011 Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; the appendix holding the assessments is called S2 in the text and Table 2 and S3 in Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which tool was used for the trials is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Haloperidol doses are printed without a per-kilogram unit (Table 3; p. 501).
reporting_issues.consequence: Doses should be checked against the primary trial before they are quoted anywhere.
